reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Belongs to a spectrum of benign, self-limiting T-cell-driven papulosquamous eruptions that runs from the chronic pole (PLC) to the acute pole (PLEVA)
PLC produces recurrent crops of small red-brown papules capped by a characteristic adherent mica-like scale that can be lifted off in one piece
Lesions appear in successive crops so that different stages coexist, usually healing with transient post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation rather than scarring
Most common in children and young adults and typically follows a relapsing-remitting course over months to years
The trunk and the proximal aspects of the limbs are the sites most often involved
Usually asymptomatic or only mildly itchy, which helps separate it from more inflammatory dermatoses
Diagnosis is clinical but supported by biopsy showing a lymphocytic interface reaction; clonality studies may be needed to distinguish it from lymphomatoid papulosis
Management is generally conservative with emollients, topical corticosteroids, and phototherapy for extensive or persistent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Pityriasis lichenoides is best regarded as a reactive, sometimes clonal, T-lymphocyte-driven process rather than a true malignancy. It is thought to represent an exaggerated hypersensitivity reaction, possibly to infectious antigens (viruses and Toxoplasma have been implicated) or to circulating immune complexes, producing a lymphocytic vasculitis with interface change at the dermo-epidermal junction. The chronic end of the spectrum shows a milder, more superficial infiltrate with parakeratotic scale, giving the persistent scaly papules of PLC, whereas the acute pole shows a denser cytotoxic response with keratinocyte necrosis. Post-inflammatory pigmentary change reflects melanin disturbance at the dermo-epidermal interface.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histopathology to confirm the interface dermatitis and characterise the infiltrate
Immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies to exclude lymphomatoid papulosis or cutaneous lymphoma
Serology for possible triggers such as Toxoplasma, Epstein-Barr virus, or HIV when clinically indicated
Full blood count and inflammatory markers in patients who are febrile or systemically unwell
Syphilis serology where secondary syphilis is a diagnostic consideration
Photographic documentation to track the evolution of successive crops
redFlags: Evolution of the acute pole into febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann disease with systemic upset
Development of persistent, infiltrated, or ulcerating plaques raising concern for cutaneous lymphoma
Atypical or clonal lymphoid infiltrate on histology requiring formal clonality assessment
Failure to settle or progressive extension despite standard therapy
reference.prognosis: Generally benign and self-limiting, although the chronic form may relapse over months or years; the great majority resolve without scarring, but rare progression to a lymphoproliferative disorder justifies long-term follow-up of atypical cases.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for guttate psoriasis or pityriasis rosea and delaying diagnostic biopsy
Overlooking the overlap with lymphomatoid papulosis, which can be histologically very similar
Assuming a single self-limited episode when the relapsing, crop-by-crop pattern is characteristic
Failing to recognise the rare but potentially serious ulceronecrotic variant
management: Reassurance about the benign, relapsing but generally self-limiting course
Emollients and topical corticosteroids to relieve itch and inflammation
Oral macrolide or tetracycline antibiotics for their anti-inflammatory effect as first-line systemic therapy
Narrowband ultraviolet B or other phototherapy for widespread or persistent disease
Topical calcineurin inhibitors as a steroid-sparing adjunct
Low-dose methotrexate reserved for refractory or extensive disease
Long-term follow-up of atypical lesions with biopsy to detect rare lymphoproliferative progression
